opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for s1 we ended up building on Qwen 2.5, specifically the 32B Instruct model, and that was mostly a practical decision rather than anything against Llama. When we started, Qwen was simply the strongest open-weight base for the things we cared about, which were math and reasoning-heavy benchmarks. Our whole premise was to see how far you can get with a really small amount of supervised fine-tuning, about a thousand carefully chosen examples. With a recipe that minimal, the starting model matters enormously. You're not teaching it new knowledge. You're mostly unlocking and shaping reasoning behavior that's already latent in the pretrained model.

Qwen had clearly seen a lot of math and reasoning-style data during pretraining. So it already had that capability sitting there, and a little bit of fine-tuning on long reasoning traces could surface it. With Llama at a comparable size, the starting point on those benchmarks was just weaker. We'd have been fighting an uphill battle, and it would have been harder to tell whether the method was working or whether we were limited by the base model.

There's also the size question. Thirty-two billion parameters was a sweet spot for us. It's big enough to have strong reasoning ability, but small enough that we could fine-tune it quickly. I think the training run was something like half an hour on sixteen H100s. The Llama lineup didn't have something at that exact size that was as competitive. You'd have had to go down to 8B or up to 70B, and 70B would have made iteration a lot slower and more expensive for an academic-style project.

I don't think there's anything fundamental here, though. I'd expect the same ideas to transfer to Llama or other families: a small, high-quality, diverse, difficult dataset plus test-time scaling tricks like budget forcing. How well it works just depends on how much reasoning ability the base model already has. That's actually one of the takeaways I find most interesting. A lot of what people call "reasoning training" is really about eliciting what pretraining already put there.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question we got a lot, actually. For the s1 work, we ended up fine-tuning Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct rather than any of the Llama models, and there were really a few reasons for that.

The first one is just raw starting capability, especially on math. When we were running the early experiments, the Qwen 2.5 models were noticeably stronger out of the box on things like MATH and AIME, and the whole premise of our work was that you could get a lot of reasoning performance with a really small amount of data — a thousand examples. If you're only doing a thousand samples of supervised fine-tuning, you're not really teaching the model new knowledge; you're mostly eliciting something that's already latent in it. So the base model matters a lot, and we wanted the strongest starting point we could get at that scale. Qwen was also what a lot of the concurrent work was building on, which made it easier to compare apples to apples.

The second reason is the size. We wanted something around 32 billion parameters, because that's big enough to actually show interesting reasoning behavior, but small enough that we could fine-tune it on 16 H100s in like 26 minutes and run all our ablations quickly. At the time, Llama's lineup had the 8B and the 70B, and nothing really in that middle range. The 8B was too weak to really see the effects we cared about, and the 70B would have made the whole thing a lot more expensive to iterate on.

And then there's also a more pragmatic element, which is that we tried some of this with other base models and the gains were just much smaller. We saw that in the ablations — if the base model hasn't seen a lot of this kind of data during pretraining, a thousand examples doesn't get you very far. So it wasn't that we had anything against Llama; it was more that for this particular recipe, where you're relying so heavily on what the model already knows, Qwen just gave us the best shot at demonstrating the effect cleanly.
